screens.title: Platform-Specific Optimization & Build Settings
screens.subtitle: Make the right build choices and optimizations for mobile, PC, and console targets

narration.text: In this chapter you'll learn how to adapt a Unity project to the performance realities of mobile, desktop, and console platforms. We'll focus on the decisions you make in Build Settings and Player Settings, the meaning of scripting backends and preprocessor directives, and the practical optimizations for textures, meshes, batching, and memory. This matters because a game that performs well on a high-end PC will often fail on a phone without careful changes: lower texture resolution, fewer draw calls, and minimized runtime allocations are common mobile requirements. You'll also see when to target ARM64, why IL2CPP is often recommended, and how texture compression formats like ASTC or ETC2 trade off quality for memory. A brief hands-on plan will show how to verify different code paths using preprocessor directives and how to profile on real devices. By the end you'll be able to configure platform settings, implement conditional code, and prioritize the optimizations that yield the largest runtime improvements. Ready to explore practical, actionable steps you can apply to your next build?

keyIdea.text: Optimization is platform-aware: choose build options and asset settings that match target hardware limits to achieve stable performance.

screens.title: What you'll be able to do
screens.subtitle: Four verified competencies for platform-aware builds

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will identify platform performance constraints, configure Unity build and player settings, implement conditional platform code, and choose asset optimizations suited to your targets. First, you will learn to map C P U, G P U, and memory differences between mobile, console, and PC, which helps you choose appropriate texture compression, polygon budgets, and frame-rate targets. Second, you'll learn how to use Unity's Build Settings and Player Settings to set the scripting backend, target architectures, and graphics APIs so the build matches the platform's requirements. Third, we'll teach you how to write and use preprocessor directives and scripting define symbols to compile different code paths, enabling platform-exclusive SDKs or development-only debug overlays. Finally, you'll practice prioritizing real optimizations — batching, occlusion culling, object pooling, and reduced allocations — and understand how to verify them on actual devices with the Unity Profiler. Each objective includes a short verification milestone so you can confirm competency during hands-on testing and builds.

screens.title: How we'll verify your skills
screens.subtitle: Concrete checks and the hands-on activity

narration.text: This page explains how you'll prove competency and where to focus during the hands-on activity. For Build Settings, verification means switching platforms in the Editor and confirming the expected scripting backend and target architecture. For platform-specific code, verification means compiling with different platform targets and seeing the appropriate code path run in the Editor or device build. For asset optimization, verification means profiling memory and draw calls before and after compression or atlasing and confirming visible quality and reduced memory usage. In the activity you'll implement PlatformQualityManager, attach a UI text element, and observe how quality level and target frame rate change when switching to Android or Windows. You will also build to a device when possible to validate real-world performance. These checks emphasize testing on actual devices with the Unity Profiler and avoiding assumptions from emulators. A successful verification shows measurable differences in quality, FPS targets, or draw-call counts when switching platform settings.

screens.title: Platform constraints: CPU, GPU, Memory
screens.subtitle: Understand the hardware trade-offs that drive platform choices

narration.text: Platform constraints are the hardware and runtime limits that determine what is reasonable to render and compute on a given device. A concrete definition: C P U capacity affects simulation and game logic, G P U capacity governs shading and draw throughput, and memory limits control texture sizes and the number of loaded assets. For example, a high-end PC can run complex shaders and many draw calls, but a mobile device often has limited G P U throughput, less R A M, and battery concerns. That means on mobile you should prefer smaller textures, compressed formats, fewer simultaneous lights, and careful allocation patterns. A common misconception is to rely on emulators or to assume that editor performance equals device performance; profiling on real hardware often exposes different bottlenecks. In practice, separate your game into scalable quality tiers so the same build can target integrated laptop GPUs and enthusiast desktop cards. A useful check is to identify the largest consumers of C P U, G P U, and memory early with profiling: one dominant hog often yields the best return on optimization. Consider this core insight: match asset and system budgets to the weakest expected hardware for a stable experience. What single bottleneck do you expect to encounter first on a phone: memory, draw calls, or GC spikes?

keyIdea.title: Why constraints matter
keyIdea.text: Design and optimization choices should prioritize the most limited resource for the target device to deliver stable frame-rates.

content.html:
Definition

Platform constraints

Limits on CPU, GPU, and memory that shape feasible rendering and runtime behavior.

  • CPU: simulation, AI, and physics cost.
  • GPU: shaders, draw calls, overdraw.
  • Memory: texture size, loaded assets, GC pressure.
Concrete example
A mobile build targets 30 FPS to reduce battery usage and uses compressed 1K textures with ASTC where supported. A desktop build uses higher-res textures and targets 60 FPS with more complex post-processing.
Practical checklist
Memory budget
Estimate texture memory and limit resident assets for lower-memory devices.
Batching & draw calls
Use atlases, static batching, and GPU instancing to reduce CPU-to-GPU overhead.
GC & allocations
Avoid per-frame allocations; use object pooling for frequently created objects.
Shader complexity
Prefer simpler mobile shaders; avoid expensive sampling and branching where possible.
Key Takeaway

Find the single largest bottleneck on your target device and focus first on reducing its cost.

screens.title: Using Build Settings & Player Settings
screens.subtitle: Select platform, configure player options, and apply platform overrides

narration.text: Build Settings and Player Settings are the primary configuration surfaces in Unity for target platform behavior. Start in File, Build Settings to select and switch your target platform. Then open Player Settings to view the platform-specific options such as Graphics APIs, scripting backend, A P I compatibility level, and target architectures. A practical flow is: choose platform, switch platform in the Editor, open Player Settings, and apply overrides like selecting IL2CPP for mobile and console or targeting ARM64. It's important to verify Graphics APIs — Unity can auto-select, but manual control helps when a specific A P I yields better performance or compatibility. Also check the stripping level and enable G P U instancing or static batching where appropriate. A common mistake is to change settings without rebuilding — many options only take effect after a platform switch and a rebuild. Examples: enabling ARM64 on Android and selecting ASTC compression for textures where supported. Always follow the flow: change, build, profile on device. Which setting will you check first on a fresh Android project? Often it's the scripting backend and target architecture to ensure native performance paths.

keyIdea.title: Build flow
keyIdea.text: Select platform, switch in Build Settings, then configure Player Settings; rebuild to apply changes and profile on device.

content.html:
Process Flow

Configure and apply build settings

  1. Select target platform in File > Build Settings and click Switch Platform to make platform-specific options available.
  2. Open Player Settings to adjust Graphics APIs, Scripting Backend, Target Architectures, and Resolution options.
  3. Set asset overrides such as texture compression formats per platform and enable batching features.
  4. Rebuild and profile on device to confirm changes actually improved performance.
Example settings
Android: IL2CPP, ARM64, ASTC textures, target 30 FPS. Windows: IL2CPP or Mono, higher quality, target 60 FPS.
Common mistake
Changing Player Settings but not rebuilding or switching platform; many options require a rebuild to take effect.
Key Takeaway

Always switch platform, set platform-specific overrides, then rebuild and profile on real hardware.

screens.title: Scripting Backends: IL2CPP vs Mono
screens.subtitle: How C# is translated and why it matters for performance

narration.text: Scripting backend determines how your C# code is compiled and executed. Mono is a managed runtime that runs C# directly, while IL2CPP converts C# into C++ and then compiles native binaries. IL2CPP often offers better performance and compatibility, especially for consoles and modern mobile platforms, because native compilation reduces runtime overhead and improves optimization opportunities. A concrete example: using IL2CPP can reduce unexpected runtime costs on platforms where Mono's garbage collector or JIT behavior is problematic. A common misconception is that IL2CPP always fixes high-level design issues — it helps with runtime efficiency, but it doesn't replace good memory management or batching. Also IL2CPP increases build times and can complicate debugging because the runtime is native. In practice, choose IL2CPP for release builds where performance and platform compatibility matter and use Mono for faster iteration in Editor when supported. Remember to test both development and release configurations because debugging or profiling instruments may behave differently with each backend. Scripting Backends: IL2CPP vs Mono means use il2cpp for release performance and compatibility; use mono for faster iteration during development when supported.. In practical terms, how c# is translated and why it matters for performance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Backend choice
keyIdea.text: Use IL2CPP for release performance and compatibility; use Mono for faster iteration during development when supported.

content.html:
Definition

Scripting backends

IL2CPP converts managed C# to native C++ binaries, improving runtime performance. Mono is a managed runtime with faster edit-time iteration.

  • IL2CPP: better runtime performance, native binary, longer build times.
  • Mono: quicker iteration, managed runtime, sometimes less performant on consoles/mobile.
Concrete example
For a console or mobile release, prefer IL2CPP to reduce runtime overhead. For rapid editor testing, Mono may be acceptable if supported.
Misconception
IL2CPP is not a substitute for fixing allocation patterns or heavy draw call counts; it complements good performance practices.
Key Takeaway

Choose IL2CPP for release builds when native performance and compatibility are critical; test both backends as part of your workflow.

screens.title: Texture Compression and Resolution
screens.subtitle: Choosing ASTC, ETC2, DXT, and resolution budgets per platform

narration.text: Texture compression reduces memory and load times by storing texture data in platform-friendly formats. On mobile, ASTC is often the best balance of quality and size where supported. ETC2 is commonly used on Android devices without ASTC support, while DXT is often used on PC. The practical decision requires checking hardware support and selecting a compression that preserves acceptable visual quality at your target memory cost. For example, swapping a 4K uncompressed texture for a compressed 1K ASTC texture can dramatically reduce memory and G P U upload time on mobile. A misconception is assuming one format fits all devices; in reality you should provide platform-specific texture overrides. Also reduce resolution where it doesn't impact perceived quality: UI elements, distant LODs, and particle textures can often be lowered without visible loss. When in doubt, profile texture memory on device and measure the visual impact of compression choices. Your goal is to balance visible fidelity and memory budget so the game runs smoothly on the weakest supported hardware. Texture Compression and Resolution means use platform-specific compression and smaller resolutions to fit memory budgets while preserving perceived visual fidelity.. In practical terms, choosing astc, etc2, dxt, and resolution budgets per platform. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Texture rule
keyIdea.text: Use platform-specific compression and smaller resolutions to fit memory budgets while preserving perceived visual fidelity.

content.html:
Comparison

Compression formats

ASTC
Flexible block sizes, high quality for mobile where supported.
ETC2
Broad Android support, decent quality, less flexibility than ASTC.
DXT
Common on PC, good tooling support.
PVRTC
Older mobile GPUs and some iOS hardware, lower quality at small sizes.
Practical example
Replace large uncompressed textures with platform-specific compressed versions and provide lower-resolution overrides for distant LODs and particle systems to cut memory use.
Misconception
Assuming a single compression format is ideal for all devices; instead, provide per-platform texture import settings and test on devices.
Key Takeaway

Choose compression per platform and test visual impact on device; smaller textures often give the best performance wins.

screens.title: Preprocessor Directives & Scripting Define Symbols
screens.subtitle: Compile platform-specific paths and debug features

narration.text: Preprocessor directives let you include or exclude code at compile time based on the active build target or custom scripting defines. The common pattern uses #if UNITY_ANDROID, #elif UNITY_STANDALONE_WIN, and #endif to select platform logic. For example, you might set QualitySettings and Application. targetFrameRate differently for mobile and desktop or include an advertising SDK only on iOS and Android. Custom scripting define symbols allow you to create flags like ENABLE_DEBUG_OVERLAY and apply them per platform in Player Settings. A common error is expecting runtime conditional checks to prevent compilation errors when platform APIs are unavailable; preprocessor directives actually remove code during compilation and thus prevent references to missing APIs. Another important point: development-only flags should be removed for release builds to avoid shipping debug tools. In practice, wrap SDK calls and platform-specific A P I usage with appropriate #if guards and verify by switching platform in Build Settings and building. This approach avoids multiple codebases and keeps platform differences explicit and testable. Preprocessor Directives & Scripting Define Symbols means use preprocessor directives and scripting defines to include only the code you need for each platform and build configuration.. In practical terms, compile platform-specific paths and debug features. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Compile-time control
keyIdea.text: Use preprocessor directives and scripting defines to include only the code you need for each platform and build configuration.

content.html:
Code example
// Example: platform-specific startup
#if UNITY_ANDROID || UNITY_IOS
    // Mobile: lower quality, target 30 FPS
    QualitySettings.SetQualityLevel(0);
    Application.targetFrameRate = 30;
#elif UNITY_STANDALONE_WIN
    // Desktop: higher quality, 60 FPS
    QualitySettings.SetQualityLevel(2);
    Application.targetFrameRate = 60;
#endif

#if ENABLE_DEBUG_OVERLAY
    // Development-only: debug overlay enabled via scripting define
    ShowDebugOverlay();
#endif
Concrete example
Wrap advertising SDK initialization with #if UNITY_IOS || UNITY_ANDROID to avoid compilation errors on other platforms.
Common mistake
Using runtime platform checks instead of compile-time guards when the API isn't available on the build target will still cause compiler errors.
Key Takeaway

Use preprocessor directives for compile-time control and scripting defines for build-configuration flags like debug overlays.

screens.title: Asset Delivery: Texture Atlases, LODs, and Mesh Optimization
screens.subtitle: Design assets so they scale across devices

narration.text: Asset delivery is about preparing textures, meshes, and levels so they consume appropriate memory and rendering costs on each target. Texture atlasing groups many small textures into one larger texture to reduce material swaps and draw calls. LOD groups let you swap high-poly meshes for simplified versions at distance. Mesh optimization includes reducing polygon counts and combining static geometry where possible. For mobile, favor atlases and fewer materials to reduce draw calls; for PC, allow higher-resolution textures and extra LOD levels. A common misconception is that reducing polygons always harms visual quality; in many scenes you can reduce unseen detail, use normal maps, or adjust LOD distances to preserve perceived fidelity while cutting runtime cost. Practical steps: create atlases for UI and repeated props, bake lightmaps for static geometry, and use LOD groups with progressively simplified meshes. Test visual fidelity on target hardware and measure draw-call reduction — combining assets into atlases and enabling static batching typically yields measurable C P U-side savings. Asset Delivery: Texture Atlases, LODs, and Mesh Optimization means atlas small textures, use lods, and reduce polygon density where it doesn't impact perceived quality to lower runtime cost.. In practical terms, design assets so they scale across devices. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Asset strategy
keyIdea.text: Atlas small textures, use LODs, and reduce polygon density where it doesn't impact perceived quality to lower runtime cost.

content.html:
Architecture pattern

Atlases, LODs, and mesh combines

Group and reduce: atlases cut material changes, LODs reduce GPU work at distance, and static combines reduce draw calls.

Atlas
Combine sprites and UI textures to reduce material swaps.
LOD
Swap meshes at distance to lower vertex and pixel cost.
Combine meshes
Static batching groups static geometry to reduce draw calls.
Concrete example
Create a UI atlas for inventory icons and combine small decorative props into a single static mesh to reduce CPU draw call overhead on mobile.
Misconception
Assuming every object benefits from combining: dynamic objects and frequently animated meshes can lose flexibility if combined incorrectly.
Key Takeaway

Prioritize atlasing for UI and repeated props, add LODs for large meshes, and combine static geometry to lower draw calls.

screens.title: Runtime Optimizations: Batching, Instancing, and Occlusion
screens.subtitle: Reduce draw calls and GPU work with batching and culling

narration.text: Reducing draw calls and unnecessary rendering is one of the highest-impact optimizations for many games. Static batching combines geometry marked as static into larger meshes, reducing C P U overhead for many static objects. Dynamic batching is useful for many small moving objects but has limitations; G P U instancing is usually the best option for many identical dynamic objects because it keeps draw calls low while preserving per-instance transforms. Occlusion culling prevents off-screen or hidden objects from being rendered at all, saving both C P U and G P U time. An example: in a crowded scene with many identical props, G P U instancing can preserve visual density while keeping draw calls low, whereas naive instantiation would create hundreds of draw calls. Misconceptions include overusing dynamic batching when G P U instancing would be more appropriate and assuming batching eliminates the need for atlases. In practice enable static batching for immovable geometry, prefer G P U instancing for large numbers of identical objects, and configure occlusion culling to match your scene complexity. Always profile before and after; these techniques reduce C P U-G P U overhead but won't fix heavy G P U pixel costs from expensive shaders.

keyIdea.title: Render savings
keyIdea.text: Use static batching for static geometry, GPU instancing for many identical objects, and occlusion culling to avoid drawing hidden objects.

content.html:
Process

Batching & culling

  1. Enable static batching for non-moving geometry to merge draw calls.
  2. Use GPU instancing for many identical moving objects to lower draw calls efficiently.
  3. Configure occlusion culling to skip rendering hidden objects behind occluders.
Concrete example
A forest scene with thousands of trees uses GPU instancing to render many trees with a single draw call per LOD, while static rocks are statically batched to minimize calls.
Misconception
Thinking batching solves expensive shader cost; batching lowers draw call overhead but doesn't reduce per-pixel shader cost.
Key Takeaway

Batching reduces CPU overhead; instancing scales identical objects efficiently; occlusion culling prevents unnecessary rendering.

screens.title: Garbage Collection & Object Pooling
screens.subtitle: Avoid runtime allocations and GC spikes on constrained devices

narration.text: Garbage collection can cause frame-time spikes when the runtime collects many short-lived objects. On memory-constrained devices, frequent allocations and deallocations increase GC frequency and produce stutter. Object pooling is the recommended pattern: pre-allocate a pool of reusable objects such as bullets, particle effects, or UI elements and reuse them instead of creating and destroying them repeatedly. For example, a mobile shooter should reuse bullet objects from a pool rather than instantiating new prefabs each frame. A common misconception is that micro-allocations are harmless; on desktop they may be tolerable, but on mobile they can cause noticeable spikes. Profiling will reveal allocation hotspots — strings, LINQ allocations, and per-frame temporary arrays are common culprits. Practical steps: avoid boxing value types, cache component references, and use pooled collections for frequently used lists. The goal is to minimize runtime allocations so the GC runs less often and more predictably, improving smoothness on low-end hardware. Garbage Collection & Object Pooling means minimize per-frame allocations, use object pools, and reduce temporary allocations to avoid gc-induced stutter.. In practical terms, avoid runtime allocations and gc spikes on constrained devices. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: GC strategy
keyIdea.text: Minimize per-frame allocations, use object pools, and reduce temporary allocations to avoid GC-induced stutter.

content.html:
Definition

Garbage Collection impacts

Frequent runtime allocations trigger GC cycles that can pause the main thread, causing frame drops.

  • Pool frequently instantiated objects to avoid allocations.
  • Avoid per-frame string concatenation and temporary collections.
  • Cache component references to avoid repeated GetComponent calls.
Concrete example
A bullet pool that pre-instantiates 50 bullets and reuses them prevents hundreds of allocations during gameplay and reduces GC pressure.
Misconception
Assuming GC spikes only happen with large assets; many small allocations can produce frequent GC activity with visible stutter.
Key Takeaway

Use object pooling and reduce temporary allocations to keep GC cycles predictable and gameplay smooth on mobile.

screens.title: Implement PlatformQualityManager (lab walkthrough)
screens.subtitle: Create the script, attach UI, and observe platform-dependent behavior

narration.text: This hands-on activity guides you through implementing PlatformQualityManager to demonstrate platform-specific quality and target frame rates. Start by creating a UI Text element named InfoText and a new script called PlatformQualityManager. Attach the script to an empty GameObject and expose the InfoText reference. In Start, set default quality and target FPS, then guard changes with preprocessor directives: if the platform is mobile, set a low quality level and target 30 FPS; if standalone, set medium or high quality and target 60 FPS. Add an Update method that writes current platform, quality name, target FPS, and actual FPS to the InfoText so you can see runtime changes. The verification step: switch platform in Build Settings to Android, run in the Editor to see the mobile code path, then switch back to PC and confirm the desktop settings. Optionally build to a device to confirm real device behavior. Be careful to guard platform-specific A P I calls with #if so compilation succeeds across platforms. This exercise demonstrates compile-time conditional behavior and the importance of testing changes with platform switches. Implement PlatformQualityManager (lab walkthrough) means write a platform-aware manager that demonstrates differing quality and fps targets per build target and verify in the editor and on device.. In practical terms, create the script, attach ui, and observe platform-dependent behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Lab goal
keyIdea.text: Write a platform-aware manager that demonstrates differing quality and FPS targets per build target and verify in the Editor and on device.

content.html:
Starter code
// PlatformQualityManager.cs (attach to GameObject)
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.UI;

public class PlatformQualityManager : MonoBehaviour
{
    public Text infoText; // Assign in Inspector

    void Start()
    {
        if (infoText == null) return;

        QualitySettings.SetQualityLevel(1);
        Application.targetFrameRate = 60;

#if UNITY_ANDROID || UNITY_IOS
        QualitySettings.SetQualityLevel(0);
        Application.targetFrameRate = 30;
#endif

        UpdateInfoText();
    }

    void Update()
    {
        UpdateInfoText();
    }

    void UpdateInfoText()
    {
        infoText.text = $"Platform: {Application.platform}\nQuality: {QualitySettings.names[QualitySettings.GetQualityLevel()]}\nTarget FPS: {Application.targetFrameRate}\nActual FPS: {Mathf.RoundToInt(1.0f / Time.unscaledDeltaTime)}";
    }
}
Steps
  1. Create InfoText UI and assign it in the Inspector.
  2. Attach script, switch platform, and run in Editor to observe different code paths.
  3. Build to device and profile with Unity Profiler for real results.
Debug tip
Use scripting define symbols for development overlays and wrap them in #if so release builds remain clean.
Key Takeaway

This lab shows how compile-time directives and Player Settings produce reproducible platform differences you can observe and measure.

screens.title: Profiling and Testing on Real Hardware
screens.subtitle: Use the Unity Profiler and device testing to find real bottlenecks

narration.text: Profiling on the actual target device is essential because emulators and the Editor rarely reflect real-world performance. Use the Unity Profiler to inspect C P U usage, G P U timings, memory allocation, and garbage collection. Connect the profiler to a device via USB or Wi-Fi and reproduce heavy gameplay scenarios to capture peaks. Pay attention to per-frame allocation spikes, the number of draw calls, and whether the G P U or C P U is the limiting factor. For example, if the profiler shows many small allocations in scripts during gameplay, focus on pooling and avoiding per-frame string operations. If the G P U shows long fragment shader times, reduce shader complexity or lower texture resolution. A common pitfall is premature optimization: profile first to identify the largest bottleneck, then optimize that area. Also beware of development build differences; profiling in development mode may allocate extra overhead. The practical workflow is: profile on device, identify a dominant hotspot, implement a targeted optimization, rebuild, and re-profile to validate the improvement. Profiling and Testing on Real Hardware means profile on real devices, identify the dominant bottleneck, make targeted changes, and re-profile to confirm gains.. In practical terms, use the unity profiler and device testing to find real bottlenecks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Profiling loop
keyIdea.text: Profile on real devices, identify the dominant bottleneck, make targeted changes, and re-profile to confirm gains.

content.html:
Workflow

Profile → identify → optimize → validate

Connect profiler
Attach to device via USB or Wi-Fi to capture real metrics.
Capture scenario
Recreate heavy gameplay to measure realistic peaks.
Analyze hotspots
Check CPU, GPU, memory, and GC timelines to find the largest cost.
Target fix
Apply a focused optimization and rebuild to validate impact.
Concrete example
If profiling shows frequent small allocations, implement object pooling for the offending systems and re-profile to compare GC frequency and frame-time stability.
Pitfall
Relying solely on editor profiling results; always confirm on physical hardware to see true performance behavior.
Key Takeaway

Profiling on device reveals the real hotspots; optimize the largest cost first, then measure the result.

screens.title: Common Optimization Areas & Priorities
screens.subtitle: What to optimize first and typical high-impact tactics

narration.text: When optimizing for multiple platforms, prioritize the changes that deliver the largest run-time improvements for the least effort. Common high-impact areas are: draw-call reduction through atlasing and batching, reducing runtime allocations to avoid GC spikes via object pooling, and lowering texture memory using appropriate compression and resolution scaling. Mesh LODs and lightmapping save real-time G P U work by reducing shading complexity. Physics optimizations like simpler colliders and reduced fixed-step frequency improve C P U-bound performance. UI optimization reduces overdraw and improves batching for large canvases. A typical workflow is to profile, list candidates, and estimate the likely improvement: start with draw calls and GC spikes because they are frequent causes of stutter on mobile. Avoid premature optimization of minor shader features until you confirm G P U fragment shading is the bottleneck. Another practical tip: use platform-specific import settings and scripting defines to compile a different feature set for constrained devices. This way you can ship one project that adapts to each platform's strengths and limits. Common Optimization Areas & Priorities means focus first on draw calls, gc spikes, and texture memory; use profiling to prioritize subsequent work.. In practical terms, what to optimize first and typical high-impact tactics. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Optimization priority
keyIdea.text: Focus first on draw calls, GC spikes, and texture memory; use profiling to prioritize subsequent work.

content.html:
Priorities

Which optimizations to start with

Draw calls
Atlas, batch, or instance to cut CPU overhead.
GC & allocations
Pool objects and reduce per-frame allocations.
Texture memory
Compress and lower resolution where acceptable.
Quick wins
Enable static batching for static geometry, atlas UI, and implement a bullet or particle pool to reduce allocations.
When not to optimize
Don't spend time on shader micro-optimizations until profiling shows the GPU fragment stage is the bottleneck.
Key Takeaway

Target the biggest measured bottleneck first. Use platform-specific settings to adapt content and code per target.

screens.subtitle: Three core ideas to keep in mind

narration.text: These three key concepts summarize the practical lessons from this chapter. First, platform-specific optimization requires understanding hardware constraints and mapping them to asset and system budgets. Second, Build Settings and Player Settings are the control surfaces where you select scripting backends, graphics APIs, and target architectures; changes must be applied with rebuilds and tested on devices. Third, preprocessor directives and scripting define symbols allow you to compile different code paths for each platform and build configuration, keeping a single project flexible. Keep these ideas close while you profile and make pragmatic, targeted changes: optimize measured hotspots first and validate improvements on real hardware. Which of these three will guide your next build decision? Keep testing and iterating until the performance matches user expectations. screens.subtitle: Three final reminders before you build

narration.text: Before you finish, remember these three practical rules. One: always test on the target hardware; emulators and the Editor are only approximations. Two: minimize runtime allocations and batch draw calls to tackle the most common mobile stutter causes. Three: use build-time control with preprocessor directives and scripting defines so you can safely include platform-only SDKs and development-only tools. Keeping these rules in mind will help you make focused, measured optimizations and avoid common pitfalls like premature optimization or shipping debug features in release builds. Ask yourself: which device will shape your lowest acceptable quality tier, and what single optimization will yield the most noticeable improvement for players on that device? Last thought
